hits.name: Avi Chawla
hits.text:
NVIDIA released a new looped transformer:

Instead of stacking more layers, it runs the same layers multiple times so a 4B model can think like a 9B one.

Here's how it works:

In a standard transformer, every token passes through a stack of decoder blocks once, and each block has its own weights.

So if you want a deeper model, you add more blocks, and the parameter count grows with the depth.

NVIDIA's Dory1.0-4B decouples the two by reusing a chunk of its layers.

The model is split into three parts:

> An input block of 8 blocks runs once and turns the tokens into a hidden state x.

> A recurrent block of 20 shared blocks runs k times, where k can be anywhere from 1 to 4.

> An output block of 8 blocks runs once on the final state, followed by the LM head.

Before every pass through the recurrent block, x is added back to the current state and the sum is L2-normalized.

This keeps the original token representation in view on every pass, instead of each pass only seeing what the previous one produced.

Both models in the diagram below store 36 blocks of weights.

The standard transformer applies each block once, while Dory applies 36 blocks at k=1, 56 at k=2, and 96 at k=4, i.e., 72, 112, and 192 physical layers from the same checkpoint.

The extra depth is actually helpful on reasoning and agentic tasks:

> SWE-bench Verified:

- at 1 loop → 50.3
- at 2 loops → 59.5
- at 4 loops → 61.8

> 12-benchmark average:

- at 1 loop → 35.17
- at 2 loops → 39.67
- at 4 loops → 40.60
- and with 2 or more loops, it beats Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 4 12B, and Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

More loops implies more compute per token, but the 4-loop model also writes 1.3x to 2.5x fewer output tokens on agentic tasks.

So 2 loops end up costing only 1.03x to 1.25x the compute of 1 loop end to end, which is why NVIDIA recommends 2 as the default.

By default, Dory keeps a separate KV cache for every loop, so at 4 loops the recurrent layers store 4x the cache.

To avoid this, it can keep only the cache from the last loop, which uses the same KV memory as a normal model with only a small change in accuracy.

One thing to note here is that looping helps the model reason over what it already knows, but it does not add knowledge.

For instance, on tasks like AA-Omniscience, accuracy stays at 10.0 whether you run 1 loop or 4, and on knowledge-heavy tasks like GPQA, Dory still trails Qwen3.5-4B.

Here's the paper: https://t.co/pdrqhdCHpZ

That said, how much memory looping costs comes down to how the KV cache is handled, so I wrote a full breakdown of how KV caching works.

It covers what gets cached during prefill, how the cache grows during decoding, and why it becomes the main memory bottleneck at long context.

Read it below.

hits.draft_en:
NVIDIA's new looped transformer gets depth without adding weights. Dory1.0-4B reuses one shared chunk of layers over and over, which lets a 4B model think like a 9B.

Setup: 8 input blocks run once, 20 shared blocks loop k times (1 to 4), 8 output blocks finish before the LM head. Each loop re-adds the original hidden state and L2-normalizes, so no pass loses sight of the input tokens.

Same 36 blocks of stored weights as a regular transformer, but up to 192 physical layers from a single checkpoint.

What the loops buy on agentic tasks and reasoning:
- SWE-bench Verified climbs 50.3 -> 59.5 -> 61.8 (1, 2, 4 loops)
- 12-benchmark average climbs 35.17 -> 39.67 -> 40.60
- with 2+ loops it outscores Qwen3.5-9B and both Gemma 4 variants

The compute bill is smaller than you'd guess: deeper runs produce 1.3x to 2.5x fewer output tokens, so 2 loops land at 1.03x to 1.25x the cost of 1 - hence NVIDIA's default of 2.

Two caveats. Per-loop KV caches mean 4x memory at 4 loops, unless you keep only the final loop's cache for near-identical accuracy. And loops sharpen reasoning, not knowledge: AA-Omniscience sits at 10.0 regardless, and GPQA still lags Qwen3.5-4B.

virals.name: George Spencer
virals.text:
One thing that can make working with AI agents frustrating is having useful information scattered across folders, research documents, and project files, then having to search for the right information manually whenever you need it.

SAG Wiki offers an interesting solution.

Imagine having a folder full of research papers, project documentation, and notes. Instead of manually going through everything, you can add that folder to SAG Wiki and turn it into a searchable knowledge base. It indexes your existing documents without model calls, requires no additional database deployment, and keeps your original files where they are. When files change, updates can be indexed incrementally.

What makes it particularly useful is its integration with agents like Claude Code and Codex through its CLI and Skills.

For example, a coding agent can retrieve relevant information from your existing project documentation before helping you work on a feature. You can also use it to find supporting information across research materials or bring relevant context into your writing workflow.

It also supports search, Q&A, and citations back to the original sources, making it easier to trace where information comes from.

I like the idea of making the knowledge you already have more accessible and useful to AI agents without introducing another complicated system to manage.

SAG Wiki is free and open source. Worth exploring if you're building AI-powered workflows.

GitHub: https://t.co/bjjCt8dp9q

outsiders.name: George Spencer
outsiders.text:
One thing that can make working with AI agents frustrating is having useful information scattered across folders, research documents, and project files, then having to search for the right information manually whenever you need it.

SAG Wiki offers an interesting solution.

Imagine having a folder full of research papers, project documentation, and notes. Instead of manually going through everything, you can add that folder to SAG Wiki and turn it into a searchable knowledge base. It indexes your existing documents without model calls, requires no additional database deployment, and keeps your original files where they are. When files change, updates can be indexed incrementally.

What makes it particularly useful is its integration with agents like Claude Code and Codex through its CLI and Skills.

For example, a coding agent can retrieve relevant information from your existing project documentation before helping you work on a feature. You can also use it to find supporting information across research materials or bring relevant context into your writing workflow.

It also supports search, Q&A, and citations back to the original sources, making it easier to trace where information comes from.

I like the idea of making the knowledge you already have more accessible and useful to AI agents without introducing another complicated system to manage.

SAG Wiki is free and open source. Worth exploring if you're building AI-powered workflows.

GitHub: https://t.co/bjjCt8dp9q
